questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: The ambiguous case of the law of sines
questions.learningObjective: Explain when the law of sines gives two triangles
questions.stem: Explain when the law of sines can produce two different triangles from the same set of measurements.

answer.exemplar: The law of sines, a over sin A equals b over sin B, determines the side b from a known a and A by b = a sin B over sin A. Because the sine of an angle and the sine of its supplement are equal, a computed value of B can match two different angles. The second candidate may or may not produce a valid triangle, which is the ambiguous case, and it occurs when a is shorter than b and A is acute.

questions.explanation: The sine function takes the same value at an angle and its supplement, so the law of sines can return two candidate angles for B. Both form triangles only when the side opposite the known angle is the shorter one.
questions.hint: Sine has the same value at an angle and its supplement.

questions.stem: Explain how the law of sines finds a missing angle when two sides and one angle are known.

answer.exemplar: The law of sines states that a over sin A equals b over sin B equals c over sin C. When the sides a and b and the angle A are known, the ratio a over sin A gives the common constant, and then sin B = b sin A over a determines the angle B by taking an inverse sine. The remaining angle follows from the fact that the angles of a triangle add to 180 degrees.

questions.explanation: The common ratio a over sin A equals b over sin B, so B is found by inverting sine on the value b sin A over a. The last angle then comes from the fact that a triangle's angles add to 180 degrees.
questions.hint: Match the ratio for the known pair with the unknown one.

answer.exemplar: The law of cosines states that c squared equals a squared plus b squared minus 2ab cos C. questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.topic: Solving triangles with the law of sines
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the law of sines can fail on extreme data
questions.stem: Explain why the law of sines needs care when a triangle contains a very large angle.

answer.exemplar: A triangle cannot have an angle of 120 degrees together with a large opposite side and a small adjacent side, because the side opposite the largest angle must be the longest side. When the law of sines produces an angle whose sum with the known angle exceeds 180 degrees, that candidate is impossible and no triangle matches the data at all.

questions.explanation: The law of sines can return a sine value that no angle can produce, or a candidate angle that pushes the angle sum past 180 degrees. Both failures mean the measurements are inconsistent.
questions.hint: Check the angle sum and the size of the sine value.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the law of cosines finds an angle from three sides
questions.stem: Explain how the law of cosines can find an angle when three sides are known.

answer.exemplar: When all three sides of a triangle are known, the law of cosines can be rearranged to isolate the cosine of the desired angle. For side c the angle C satisfies cos C = (a squared plus b squared minus c squared) over 2ab, and the inverse cosine of that ratio returns C in degrees. Unlike the law of sines this route gives a single unambiguous angle.

questions.explanation: Solving the cosine law for a single angle removes the two-candidate problem of the sine law. The inverse cosine then returns the unique angle between 0 and 180 degrees that fits the three sides.
questions.hint: Isolate the cosine of the angle and invert it.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sine value does not determine a unique angle
questions.stem: Explain why a given sine value does not determine a unique angle.

answer.exemplar: The sine function is not one-to-one over a full 360 degree cycle because it rises to one, falls to minus one and rises again, so the same sine value appears at two different angles in every cycle. The inverse sine therefore needs a restricted domain, usually minus 90 to 90 degrees, to be a genuine function. Working with the equation instead of the function restores both branches.

questions.explanation: Because sine rises and falls within each cycle, one sine value corresponds to two angles. The inverse sine fixes this by returning only the angle in its principal range.
questions.hint: Sine takes each value twice within one cycle.

questions.subject: PRECALCULUS
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to solve a secant equation
questions.stem: Explain how to find all angles whose secant equals a given value.

answer.exemplar: The equation sec theta = c is equivalent to cos theta = 1 over c, so solving it reduces to a cosine equation. For a positive value of c the cosine must be positive, giving an acute angle theta = the inverse cosine of 1 over c and a fourth-quadrant partner of 360 minus theta. The inverse secant names only the principal one of these.

questions.explanation: Reciprocating the secant value gives the cosine value, and the cosine equation has two solutions in a full cycle. The inverse secant reports only the principal branch of that pair.
questions.hint: Reciprocate the value and solve the cosine equation.
